The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Liberal Democrats Manifesto 2015 - Summary

## Stronger Economy, Fairer Society: Opportunity for Everyone

The Liberal Democrats present their vision for Britain built on five key pledges: balancing the budget fairly, cutting taxes by raising the Personal Allowance to £12,500, investing £8 billion in the NHS with equal care for mental health, protecting education funding from nursery to age 19, and safeguarding the environment through five green laws.

### Economic Vision

The manifesto emphasises responsible fiscal management while ensuring fairness. The party commits to eliminating the structural deficit by 2017/18 through a balanced approach of spending restraint and targeted tax increases on the wealthy, banks, and polluters—explicitly rejecting the Conservative approach of cuts-only austerity. Once books are balanced, public spending will grow with the economy.

The economic strategy centres on building a high-skill, low-carbon economy through industrial strategy, infrastructure investment, and innovation. Key proposals include doubling research spending, expanding apprenticeships, completing broadband rollout, and major rail investment including HS2. The Green Investment Bank will be expanded to stimulate £100 billion in low-carbon investment.

### Fairness in Taxation and Welfare

The party pledges to continue raising the tax-free Personal Allowance while ensuring the wealthy contribute fairly through reforms to Capital Gains Tax, a High Value Property Levy, and tough action on corporate tax avoidance. Welfare reforms focus on Universal Credit implementation while protecting the vulnerable, with opposition to benefit freezes for the poorest. The "triple lock" pension guarantee will be enshrined in law.

### Public Services

Education funding will be protected from early years through age 19, with qualified teachers guaranteed in every classroom. The NHS receives commitment of £8 billion additional funding, with £500 million specifically for transforming mental health services to achieve genuine parity with physical health. Health and social care will be integrated through pooled budgets.

### Environmental Commitment

Five green laws form the centrepiece of environmental policy: a Nature Act, Resource Efficiency Act, Green Transport Act, Zero Carbon Britain Act, and Green Buildings Act. The party commits to zero net greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 and 60% renewable electricity by 2030.

### Constitutional Reform and Civil Liberties

The manifesto champions devolution, implementing Smith Commission proposals for Scotland, further Welsh powers, and "Devolution on Demand" for English localities. Electoral reform remains central, with support for STV voting and votes at 16. Civil liberties are protected through opposition to the "Snooper's Charter," a Digital Bill of Rights, and retention of the Human Rights Act.

### International Outlook

The party firmly supports EU membership while advocating reform, with commitment to an in/out referendum only if treaty changes transfer sovereignty. International development spending of 0.7% of national income is maintained in law, while defence policy includes moving to reduced nuclear submarine patrols as a step toward disarmament.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2015: Summary

## Core Promise: Britain Can Be Better

The 2015 Labour Manifesto is built on the fundamental belief that Britain only succeeds when working people succeed. It opens with a "Budget Responsibility Lock" – a commitment that every policy is fully funded without additional borrowing, with deficits cut annually and national debt falling.

## Economic Vision

Labour presents itself as both pro-business and pro-worker, rejecting the Conservative view that economic success depends on "a privileged few at the top." The manifesto argues that the link between national prosperity and family finances has been broken, with wages falling dramatically since 2010 while millions work in low-paid, insecure jobs.

Key economic pledges include: raising the National Minimum Wage to over £8 by 2019; banning exploitative zero-hours contracts; introducing a 50p tax rate for those earning over £150,000; abolishing non-dom status; cutting tuition fees to £6,000; and establishing a British Investment Bank to support small businesses.

## Public Services

The NHS is positioned as Labour's "proudest achievement," with pledges to invest £2.5 billion more than Conservatives to recruit 8,000 GPs, 20,000 nurses, and 3,000 midwives – funded by a Mansion Tax on properties over £2 million. The manifesto promises to repeal Conservative privatisation plans and integrate physical health, mental health, and social care into a unified system.

On education, Labour commits to protecting the entire education budget, guaranteeing qualified teachers, capping class sizes for young children, and creating gold-standard technical education through a new Technical Baccalaureate.

## Families and Communities

The manifesto emphasises support for working families through expanded childcare, doubled paternity leave, and building 200,000 homes annually. It pledges to abolish the "cruel" Bedroom Tax while maintaining immigration controls, requiring EU migrants to wait two years before claiming benefits.

## Devolution and Democracy

Labour promises the "biggest devolution of power in a hundred years" through an English Devolution Act transferring £30 billion to city and county regions, alongside implementing further Scottish and Welsh devolution. It commits to votes at 16, replacing the House of Lords with an elected Senate, and a Constitutional Convention.

## International Stance

The manifesto affirms EU membership as "central to our prosperity and security" while promising reform. It maintains commitment to NATO, nuclear deterrence, and international development spending, while placing climate change at the heart of foreign policy.

## Conclusion

Labour frames the election as a choice between an economy serving "a privileged few" or one rebuilt for working people – promising hope without "promising the earth," with all commitments fully funded.
